The Story of King Surat

I bow with devotion to the feet of Lord Jina, worshipped by the gods, and I write the story of King Surat.

Surat was the king of Ayodhya. He had five hundred wives, among whom the chief queen held the title of Mahadevi Sati. The king loved Sati above all others and spent his days and nights absorbed in sensual pleasures, neglecting the affairs of state entirely. He had instructed the guard at the inner quarters: "Only inform me when something of special importance arises or when a saint or holy person visits. Otherwise, never disturb me."

One day, by the ripening of good karma, two monks named Damdatt and Dhammrucci, who had observed a month-long fast, came to the royal palace seeking alms. Seeing them, the doorkeeper went to the king and announced the monks' arrival. At that moment the king was painting a tilak on the lotus face of his beloved Sati. He said to her, "My dear, until your tilak dries, I shall quickly feed the monks and return." With these words, the king went and seated the monks with devotion on high seats, and with nine-fold worship served them sacred food — which bestows the highest happiness.

Truly, it is through charity, worship, vows, and fasting that lay devotees shine; those who lack these are like a fruitless tree, devoid of purpose. Therefore the wise should always practise giving to worthy recipients, worshipping the Jinas, and observing vows and fasts according to their capacity.

While the king earned merit by feeding the monks, his beloved queen Sati was furious that these monks had interrupted her sensual enjoyment. Without considering right or wrong, she began reviling them and hurling every manner of abuse at the holy men. The saints' saying is not in vain: "What one hand gives, the other takes away."

The queen received the fruit of her intense sinful karma at that very moment. Leprosy broke out upon her body. Her entire skin turned black, and a foul stench emanated from her. The Acharyas say: it is better to drink the halahal poison, which brings suffering in just one lifetime, than to revile saints, which brings misery birth after birth. For true saints are adorned with vows, fasting, and moral conduct, and they show the path to genuine self-welfare. To revile them is the gravest of sins.

The queen's beauty and health were destroyed in an instant. The king, who had been so devoted to her, now found her presence unbearable. She who had cursed the monks for interrupting her pleasure was now shunned by all. She suffered greatly and eventually repented for her sin, but the damage was done.

This story teaches that reviling saints and holy beings brings swift and terrible consequences. No amount of worldly power or beauty can protect one from the fruit of such a sin. The wise should always honour those who walk the path of dharma, for even a moment of disrespect can undo a lifetime of merit.
